item_name: False Positives on Non-Native English Speakers (Liang et al. Stanford 2023)
creators_or_institution: Weixin Liang, Mert Yuksekgonul, Yining Mao, Eric Wu, James Zou — Stanford University (Department of Biomedical Data Science and affiliated departments)
background_story: In April 2023, a team of Stanford researchers led by PhD student Weixin Liang and professor James Zou noticed a troubling pattern: AI detection tools, widely promoted as solutions to academic dishonesty, were systematically flagging text written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated. The team designed a controlled study comparing TOEFL essays (written by non-native English speakers for language proficiency testing) against GPT-generated text, testing seven of the most widely used AI detectors. The results were alarming and the paper was published in the journal Patterns (Cell Press) in July 2023, becoming one of the most-cited papers on AI detection limitations.
how_it_works: Research methodology: (1) Collected 91 TOEFL exam essays written by non-native English speakers (publicly available dataset). (2) Generated AI-written essays on the same TOEFL prompts using ChatGPT. (3) Submitted both sets to seven widely-used AI detectors: GPTZero, Originality.ai, Writer.com AI detector, Copyleaks, Content at Scale, Crossplag, and ZeroGPT. (4) Analyzed false positive rates (human TOEFL essays classified as AI) vs true positive rates (GPT essays correctly classified as AI). (5) Also compared against US 8th-grade student essays (native English speakers). Key finding: detectors classified TOEFL essays as AI at dramatically higher rates than 8th-grade essays, despite both being clearly human-written.
accuracy_or_effectiveness: The study found that all seven tested AI detectors showed systematic bias: 61.3% of TOEFL non-native-speaker essays were classified as AI-generated across all seven detectors. For US 8th-grade native-speaker essays, false positive rates were near zero. The paper also showed that simple 'literary language prompting' (asking ChatGPT to rewrite its output using more varied vocabulary) reduced AI detection rates to near zero — demonstrating that detectors can be easily bypassed while also falsely flagging innocent ESL students.
limitations_and_criticisms: The study exposed: (1) AI detectors conflate 'simple, predictable writing' with 'AI writing' — these are not equivalent. (2) Non-native English speakers naturally use simpler, more predictable vocabulary and sentence structures due to language proficiency constraints. (3) This creates a serious equity problem: AI detectors disproportionately harm international students, second-language learners, and students from under-resourced educational backgrounds. (4) The same detectors that miss AI-generated text with varied vocabulary correctly flag human text with simple vocabulary — exactly backwards from academic integrity goals. (5) Deploying these detectors in multilingual or diverse student populations creates discriminatory outcomes.
false_positive_rate: 61.3% of non-native-speaker TOEFL essays were classified as AI-generated (across 7 detectors). Near 0% false positive rate for native English speaker (US 8th-grade) essays. This is the most significant documented equity disparity in AI detection performance.
notable_cases_or_examples: The Markup (August 2023): 'AI Detection Tools Falsely Accuse International Students of Cheating' — directly cited the Liang et al. findings and reported on real cases — https://themarkup.org/machine-learning/2023/08/14/ai-detection-tools-falsely-accuse-international-students-of-cheating

UC Berkeley D-Lab published an analysis based on the paper: 'The Creation of Bad Students: AI Detection for Non-Native English Speakers' — https://dlab.berkeley.edu/news/creation-bad-students-ai-detection-non-native-english-speakers
Vanderbilt University cited equity concerns (including this type of bias) when disabling Turnitin's AI detector in August 2023
Paper published in Patterns (Cell Press) July 2023, and simultaneously reported on ScienceDaily: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2023/07/230710113921.htm
The paper prompted multiple universities to revise or abandon AI detector use policies for international student populations
key_publications_or_sources: Liang, W., Yuksekgonul, M., Mao, Y., Wu, E., Zou, J. (2023). 'GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers'. Patterns, 4, Article 100779. Cell Press. DOI: https://www.cell.com/patterns/fulltext/S2666-3899(23)00130-7
current_status_2024_2026: The Liang et al. (2023) paper has become one of the most cited arguments against using AI detectors for academic misconduct proceedings. As of 2025-2026, it has influenced: (1) Vanderbilt, Michigan State, Northwestern, UT's decisions to disable Turnitin AI detection. (2) Multiple professional organizations' guidelines advising against AI detectors as standalone evidence. (3) The paper is widely cited in educational technology policy discussions. The core bias problem has not been technically resolved — newer detector models have not demonstrated elimination of the ESL false positive bias.
